title: Draupadi's question
hook: Vidura tells the hall of Prahlada, a father who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely
carry: staying silent shares in the wrong

segments.voice: Yesterday Karna argued from the elders' silence, and the cloth kept coming. She is still standing.

The heap of cloth lies on the floor. The hall is shaken, and still no one has answered Draupadi. So Vidura stands, and instead of an argument, he tells an old story. It's about a judge asked to decide a case in which his own son was one of the two sides. The question for him was simple and terrible: will you tell the truth if it costs your own child?
screen: `STILL NO ONE HAS ANSWERED.` → `VIDURA TELLS A STORY.` → `A JUDGE, AND HIS OWN SON.`

segments.voice: Vidura begins with the hall. Draupadi has asked a question, he says, and it must be answered. Someone who knows the answer and stays silent shares in the wrong, and so does someone who answers falsely. Then the story. Two young men, Virochana, Prahlada's son, and Sudhanvan, a Brahmin's son, quarreled over which of them was the greater, and staked their lives on it. They went to Prahlada, Virochana's own father, to judge between them. Sudhanvan warned him: answer falsely, or not at all, and you'll suffer for it. Troubled, Prahlada went to the sage Kashyapa and asked what becomes of one who won't answer, or who answers wrongly. Kashyapa told him such a person carries a heavy burden of wrong. So Prahlada came back and gave his verdict, against his own son. Sudhanvan is the greater, he said, and Sudhanvan's father is greater than I am. And Sudhanvan, moved by that honesty, gave Virochana's life back to his father. Then Vidura turns to the kings and elders and says, in effect: you've heard it. Now think, and answer her. Prahlada had every reason to tilt the truth: it was his own son. He didn't. The kings in the hall have far less at stake, and still they won't speak. The telling says that even after Vidura's story, the kings said nothing at all.
screen: `VIDURA: SILENCE SHARES IN THE WRONG.` · `TWO YOUNG MEN, ONE QUARREL.` · `PRAHLADA JUDGES AGAINST HIS SON.` · `STILL THE KINGS SAY NOTHING.` · then, large: `ANSWER HER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a question, asked of you or of a group you're part of, that's still waiting for an honest answer, maybe one that would cost a friendship, some pride, or an advantage for your own side. Don't answer it now; just see quietly what the honest answer would be, the way Prahlada had to. If you pray, you can bring that question into your prayer; if not, simply rest in the quiet.
Draupadi's question. Vidura tells of Prahlada, who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely, and asks the hall to answer her.
Your line: staying silent shares in the wrong. Vidura said it out loud, to a silent hall. That's day seven hundred seventy-four.

fork.setup: you're Prahlada. your son and a Brahmin's son ask you to judge between them, and the truth is against your son. what do you do?
options: tell the truth, against your son.
fork.reveal: after asking the sage Kashyapa, he judges for Sudhanvan, and Sudhanvan gives Virochana's life back to his father.

original.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, what Prahlada chose over his own son's cause.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old fable dropped into the middle of a crisis.
what it means: a story about answering truly when it costs your own, told to a hall that won't answer.
what a scholar hears: the poem meets the hall's silence with a story inside a story, and the inner story judges the outer hall.
recall: a game of dice, played for stakes

chat.says: Why did Vidura tell a story about Prahlada in the middle of all that?
options: Prahlada judged against his own son rather than lie; the kings risked far less.
To calm the kings down so Draupadi could slip quietly out of the hall.
Because Prahlada had once judged a famous game of dice between kings.
chat.meaning: Vidura said silence shares in the wrong. Prahlada told the truth even against his own son, yet the kings still said nothing.

Prahlada.meaning: Virochana's father, who judges against his own son

Virochana.meaning: Prahlada's son, one of the two young men who quarrel

Sudhanvan.meaning: a Brahmin's son who quarrels with Virochana

Kashyapa.meaning: the sage Prahlada asks for counsel

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Vidura's address to the assembly; the story of Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan, and Prahlada's question to Kashyapa; the kings' silence)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Vidura's teaching that one who knows and does not answer, and one who answers falsely, both incur sin (Ganguli gives proportions of the sin; left out).

Confirm the Prahlada story details: Virochana and Sudhanvan quarrel (over a maiden in some tellings; left out) and stake their lives; Prahlada consults Kashyapa; Prahlada says Sudhanvan and Angiras (Sudhanvan's father) are superior; Sudhanvan returns Virochana's life.
Confirm that the kings said nothing after Vidura spoke.
Placement: the script follows the order in which Ganguli has Vidura speak after the disrobing; confirm.
